name: PT Tigaraksa Satria Tbk

frontmatter.title: Tigaraksa Satria — a sound distributor inside a closed share register
frontmatter.summary: Tigaraksa is a scaled Indonesian consumer-goods distributor: a wide outlet network, a fresh principal pipeline and a net-cash balance sheet. Margins are thin but stable and most profit reaches shareholders as dividends. Our fundamental value sits well above the price, but ADTV is far below the house liquidity floor and one family controls almost all the shares, so the rule-based discount holds the target at the market. HOLD.
thesis: Distribution scale is the franchise — the group reaches a very large outlet base through its own network, and consumer products carry almost all of revenue [S10, S6].
The top line is recovering faster than the company's own record of delivery suggests it should; we model growth below the published target but above the industry rate the deck carries [S4, S10].
Gross margin is a thin, defensive spread rather than a lever; we hold it flat instead of extrapolating either the recent recovery or the multi-year drift [S7, S4].

The gap between fundamental value and the price is a governance and liquidity gap, not an operating one — one family controls the register, the public float is small and the traded line is below the house liquidity floor [S6, S0].

A dated regulatory requirement now sits behind the register — the free float must reach the exchange minimum by 31 March 2029, which makes a corporate action a base-rate possibility rather than a hope [S13].
Net cash and a high payout make the dividend the real return; we model the record payout rather than the stated floor [S6, S7].

catalysts.event: Payment of the declared fiscal 2026 interim dividend
FY2026 audited results and the proposed final dividend
Annual general meeting approves the fiscal 2026 dividend
Public expose with the fiscal 2027 budget and the principal pipeline
Deadline to meet the exchange's minimum free-float requirement under Rule I-A

blocks.text: We initiate Tigaraksa Satria at **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of Rp4,605 against a last price of Rp4,720, a total return of 4.0% including the dividend we model for the year ahead. The target is not our estimate of what the business is worth. It is our estimate of what a minority holder can expect to realise: the pre-discount value of Rp6,579 a share, less the liquidity discount the house schedule applies because the stock trades IDR12.3m a day — the deepest ADTV band in the rule [S0].

The variant view is about the top line, not the margin. The share price implies FY2027E revenue growth of -0.6% — a one-year rate, because the reverse DCF holds the rest of our growth path at base and flexes only the first full forecast year — a stagnation case for a distributor whose revenue we model at IDR14,467.5bn for FY2026E and which added new principals through 2025 [S10, S4]. We think the market is extrapolating a poor budget year and a soft consumer into the long run, while the first nine months of 2026 already show revenue ahead of the prior year by a double-digit margin [S4]. On the operating evidence the shares are cheap.

What moves the value is the spread, not the volume: a one-point change in gross margin is worth more to the target than several points of revenue growth, which is why the sensitivity table below carries a wide band on that axis [S4, S7]. The second driver is the discount itself, and it has a precise mechanism: the house schedule in fund rules cuts the target by 30.0% whenever three-month ADTV is below its top band, which is the case here at IDR12.3m a day [S0]. That is a tradability haircut, separate from the 0.5% governance premium inside the cost of equity; it is not a second charge for the same fact, and the report keeps the two effects apart in the valuation section. The discount is the difference between a BUY and a HOLD here.

We are therefore not rejecting the business; we are pricing the register. A holder who can buy size without moving the price is buying a net-cash distributor at a discount to our fundamental value with a dividend yield above the deposit rate. A public-market investor cannot do that in size. But the register is no longer static: the free float — 7.5% scripless plus 0.2% scrip — is below the exchange's 15.0% minimum, and for an issuer of this market value the deadline to reach it is 31 March 2029, so a sell-down, placement or rights issue is a live possibility in the forecast window [S13]. HOLD, with the rating driven by the gap between operating value and realisable value rather than by the operating outlook.

Tigaraksa Satria was founded in 1986 and has been listed since 1990; its stated field of business is the sale and distribution of consumer products, run through five units — consumer products distribution, powder manufacturing and packing, a smart-family-product trading arm, an LPG refill and kitchen-equipment business, and a cold-storage logistics provider [S10, S6]. The company is an independent distributor, not a brand owner: it buys finished goods from principals, takes title and inventory risk, and sells them into modern and general trade, medical channels and food service [S10].

Consumer products are the whole company for practical purposes. External food and consumer-product sales were IDR12,637.2bn of consolidated revenue of IDR13,069.1bn in fiscal 2025, with the logistics, gas and trading units contributing small single-digit percentages each and intercompany sales eliminated on consolidation [S6, S10]. That mix matters for the valuation: this is a spread business on other companies' brands, so revenue is a function of principals' volumes and pricing, and gross margin is a function of the distribution fee embedded in the chain.

The network is the asset. The group reports coverage of 206,371 outlets, split across mini-market key accounts, modern-trade key accounts, modern-trade independents, medical outlets, food service, e-commerce and the general-trade base that supplies the majority of the count [S10]. It serves those outlets from main and branch warehouses across several regions with its own fleet and a layer of subdistributors and agents, which is what allows a principal to hand over national distribution rather than a single island [S10, S6].

The principal list is diversified but not evenly. The company carries 16.0 principals in food and beverage alongside baby and child nutrition and non-food lines, and it added new principals during 2025, including a savoury-snacks brand from the fourth quarter, whose contribution was still small in the year but which management presents as a growth driver for the following year [S10, S6]. Growth strategy is explicitly "optimised growth": add outlets, improve distribution processes, win new principals and lean on principal-funded promotion, with cost control rather than price as the margin lever [S10].

Ownership is concentrated. PT Penta Widjaja Investindo holds 36.2%, PT Sarana Ledaun 29.3% and PT Widjajatunggal Sejahtera 25.4% — three Widjaja-family vehicles that together control the company — while scripless public shareholders hold 7.5% and scrip holders a further 0.2%, so the public float is 7.5% on the exchange's registry [S6, S0]. The president director is Lianne Widjaja and the board includes independent commissioners and directors, but the controlling shareholders set the strategy and the dividend [S10, S6].

An independent distributor in Indonesian fast-moving consumer goods earns a percentage spread on goods it buys and resells, so its revenue scales with the brands it carries and its margin depends on negotiated terms, rebates and the cost of moving stock across an archipelago. The structural threat is disintermediation: large principals periodically take distribution in-house where volume justifies it, and modern-trade chains increasingly buy direct. The structural defence is density — the cost per outlet visit falls as coverage rises, and a principal that wants national reach quickly has few partners that can deliver it.

The demand pool is Indonesian food and beverage, which grew 7.0% in the first quarter of 2026, faster than the national economy and supported by Ramadan and Idulfitri demand and by rice and edible-oil production [S8, S11]. Household consumption is the largest component of GDP, but the company's own review describes purchasing power in 2025 as broadly flat year on year, with consumers shopping more selectively and businesses cautious on stock [S6]. That combination — a growing category with a cautious consumer — is exactly the environment in which a distributor's volume growth comes from adding principals and outlets rather than from underlying consumption.

Cost is the live pressure. The industry association flags rupiah weakness and international freight as the two worries that dominate members' planning, with container costs to some destinations up several-fold and importers hunting alternative routes and suppliers [S9]. For Tigaraksa the transmission is indirect but real: the principals whose goods it distributes face wheat, dairy, packaging and freight costs, and their ex-factory prices set the base on which the distributor earns its spread. The house decks, both as of 9 November 2026, carry the cost path by year rather than in one direction: wheat at US$294/t in FY2026E and US$294/t in FY2027E against a spot of US$217/t; CPO at US$1,135/t in FY2026E, below the US$1,180/t spot, rising to US$1,240/t in FY2027E; and the rupiah at Rp17,570/USD in FY2026E, below the Rp18,039/USD spot, before Rp18,350/USD in FY2027E. So the input path is elevated on wheat, flat-to-up on CPO and up on the dollar after a first-year dip, which is why we model a front-loaded cost drag followed by a second leg rather than a single tailwind [S9, S8].

The competitive field is layered. At the top, large principals run their own distribution where volume justifies the fixed cost; below them a long tail of regional distributors competes for the same outlets; and modern-trade chains increasingly buy direct. Tigaraksa's position is as a national independent with breadth that few regional players can match, and the company argues that documented, transparent principal terms are a differentiator against other distributors [S6, S10]. The company discloses outlet coverage and principal counts rather than a market-share series, so we do not put a share number in this report; the evidence for scale is the network itself [S10].

Five-forces reading for consumer-goods distribution in Indonesia. Supplier power is high and rising: a handful of multinational principals can move a large share of a distributor's revenue, and they renegotiate terms periodically. Buyer power is fragmented at the outlet level but concentrated in modern trade, which negotiates hard and pays slowly. New entrants face a density barrier rather than a capital barrier — the warehouses are not expensive, the route economics are. Substitutes are the principals' own vans and direct-to-retail platforms. Rivalry is intense but local, so scale advantages persist within a region rather than nationally.

Regulation touches the business through product registration, halal certification, import licensing and labelling for the goods it carries, and through the labour and logistics rules that govern warehouses and fleets; none of these is a first-order driver of the spread, but a change in import permits for dairy or cereal inputs passes straight into principal pricing [S9]. The macro deck's rupiah and policy-rate paths matter more than any single regulation, because they set both the cost of imported content and the purchasing power of the consumer the network serves [S9, S6].

The moat is real but narrow. Distribution density, cold-chain capability and medical-channel access are genuine barriers to a new entrant winning a national mandate, and they support the durability of the spread. They do not confer pricing power: the distributor negotiates a fee, and the principal retains the brand and the consumer relationship. That is why we treat the franchise as a steady compounder of volume with a defensible but capped margin, not as a brand with pricing power [S6, S10].

Revenue has gone sideways for four years: IDR12,977.5bn in fiscal 2022, IDR14,210.1bn in fiscal 2023, IDR13,363.7bn in fiscal 2024 and IDR13,069.1bn in fiscal 2025, a small decline in the latest year as existing principals slowed and the new mandates landed too late to move the total [S7, S10]. Gross margin drifted from 10.9% to 9.0% over the same period, which is the single most important fact in the file: the company has been buying revenue growth with spread, and the spread has not stopped compressing until the current year [S7].

The fiscal 2025 result is a thin-spread year: gross profit of IDR1,182.6bn on revenue of IDR13,069.1bn, operating expenses of IDR805.7bn, operating profit of IDR376.8bn, net profit attributable to shareholders of IDR408.8bn and earnings per share of Rp445 [S7]. We restate the pack here rather than carrying its error forward. The data pack prints an overstated operating profit because it folds most of the non-operating line into opex: the audited statement shows operating expenses of IDR805.7bn (selling plus G&A) and a separate non-operating "others, net" of IDR108.6bn, which reconciles to profit before tax of IDR494.4bn only when that income sits below the operating line [S7]. Our history is rebuilt from the filing for both fiscal years: operating profit for FY2025 is IDR376.8bn and for FY2024 IDR430.5bn [S7, F41, F44]. Depreciation and amortisation is restated the same way, to IDR103.3bn from the notes' fixed-asset, right-of-use and intangible charges against the pack's smaller figure, which lifts the FCFF add-back and puts EBITDA at IDR480.1bn [S7, F42]. That last change is not cosmetic: the EV/EBITDA cross-check in the valuation section now runs on the restated trailing EBITDA, and the calibration test compares our FY2026 margin with the audited FY2025 margin, so both moved when the defect was corrected.

The first nine months of 2026 are a clear improvement. Revenue reached IDR10,636.7bn against IDR9,518.7bn a year earlier, gross profit IDR1,008.3bn, profit before tax IDR359.0bn and net profit IDR286.0bn [S4]. The margin recovery is real — gross margin rose despite higher wheat and CPO costs — but it was bought with selling expense of IDR506.6bn against IDR404.9bn, so the operating spread is doing the work while distribution spending grows faster than sales [S4]. That is the trade we underwrite: principals fund promotion, the distributor spends to keep shelf presence, and the net margin stays in the low single digits.

Our forecast carries revenue growth of 10.7% in fiscal 2026, then 7.0% in fiscal 2027 — the industry deck's nominal rate, not above it — easing to 5.5% by fiscal 2030 and 4.0% in perpetuity [S4, S10]. We are below the company's own target because the 2025 plan was missed badly — realised revenue was 86.2% of budget — and we are at, not above, the category's growth rate from fiscal 2027 because the record does not support more: revenue went from IDR12,977.5bn in fiscal 2022 to IDR13,069.1bn in fiscal 2025, and fiscal 2025 revenue was 97.8% of the prior year's, so there is no disclosed principal or outlet bridge for sustained outgrowth once the 2026 recovery annualises [S7, S10, S8]. The sensitivity grid below shows the value two points slower on that axis, a five-per-cent medium-term path. Gross margin is held at 9.8%, the level that reproduces the reported nine-month margin after the deck's cost drag, rather than extrapolating either the recovery or the multi-year decline [S4, S7]. Operating expenses fade from 6.7% of revenue to 6.4% on scale, and the effective tax rate stays at 19.0%, the rate the accounts show being paid [S7].

Cash conversion is the weak point. In the first nine months of 2026 operations consumed IDR282.6bn of cash against a net profit of IDR286.0bn, because payables that had funded the balance sheet in 2025 reversed and inventory rebuilt ahead of the fourth quarter [S4]. The 2025 cash-flow statement shows the mirror image, with a large working-capital release flattering free cash flow in that year [S7]. Neither year is representative: the underlying business converts most of its profit to cash over a cycle, but the swing is wide and we model working capital at 4.5% of revenue, between the two readings, so the forecast does not rely on a repeat of either [S0, S7].

The balance sheet is a genuine strength, but it has moved since the year-end and the report uses the latest date. At 30 September 2026 the group held IDR718.3bn of cash and IDR246.7bn of short-term investments against IDR34.0bn of current and IDR49.9bn of non-current bank borrowings, plus lease liabilities of IDR31.9bn and IDR43.0bn [S4]. The liquid pool — cash plus short-term investments — is therefore smaller than the IDR1,677.4bn the pack shows at 31 December 2025: it fell over the nine months, and the cash-flow statement explains how. Operations consumed IDR282.6bn, the group paid IDR261.8bn of dividends to shareholders and IDR31.9bn of lease principal, and it funded that by redeeming short-term investments, which is why cash on its own rose while the pool fell [S4]. This is a working-capital and distribution year, not a leverage story: borrowings are a working-capital facility and the group is still in net cash on either definition [S4, S7].

The model's valuation bridge uses the 30 September 2026 position, so the equity value in the valuation section starts from that net cash, not from the year-end figure — the difference is worth a material part of the target and a reader comparing this report with the December balance sheet would otherwise find a gap of several hundred billion rupiah. The four lines above sum to IDR158.8bn of gross borrowings, against cash and short-term investments of IDR718.3bn plus IDR246.7bn, so net cash at that date is IDR806.2bn; the filing's total liability line reconciles with no other borrowing caption, which is why we treat those four lines as the whole of the debt. The data pack carries a larger gross-debt figure with no matching borrowing line in the filing, so the model's balance-sheet debt is restated from the filing and the filing's net cash, not the pack's, is what enters the equity bridge [S4, S0].

Capital allocation is dividend-first. The stated policy is a floor of 35.0% of net profit with a formula linked to cost of equity, and the record is well above the floor: 68.5% on fiscal 2024 earnings, with the two prior years in the low sixties to low seventies, and a dividend per share of Rp300 [S6]. Fiscal 2025 paid Rp315 a share against EPS of Rp445, close to the 70.0% payout we model — in line with the latest actual rather than with the policy floor, and consistent with a net-cash balance sheet [S0, S6]. That gives a forecast dividend per share of Rp302 and a yield of 6.4% at the current price [S0, S6]. Capital expenditure is small — the public expose shows IDR29.0bn realised in fiscal 2025, while the pack's IDR73.5bn also carries right-of-use additions and intangibles — so the capital intensity of the franchise is low and the dividend is not funded by leverage [S10, S7].
Earnings-quality screens, run before the estimates were committed:

items: **Accruals and cash conversion.** Negative operating cash flow in the first nine months against positive net profit is an optics-class flag, not a manipulation-class one: it is explained by payables timing and inventory, and the prior year shows the offsetting release [S4, S7]. We would treat a second consecutive year of negative operating cash flow as a red flag.

**Divergence.** Selling expense is growing faster than revenue while gross margin recovers, so operating leverage is coming from the spread, not from cost discipline [S4]. Receivables and inventory are not outgrowing revenue on the disclosed balances [S7].
**IDX regime.** We checked the annual report and the public expose and found no disclosure of special-monitoring status or notation letters; the shares trade on the main board [S6, S10].

**Related parties.** The notes state there were no sales to related parties and no related-party receivables in 2025 or 2024; the only related-party flows disclosed are key-management compensation [S7]. Purchases from the largest supplier, at IDR7.20tn against cost of revenue of IDR11,886.6bn, are an arm's-length concentration risk rather than a related-party one — optics class, disclosed, but material to the spread if terms moved [S7].

**Structure.** Concentrated family control, a small free float and a long dividend record; no serial rights issues, no dilutive instruments and no pledge of the controlling blocks disclosed in the ownership section [S6].

blocks.text: A distributor with a stable spread, low capital intensity and a net-cash balance sheet is a cash-flow asset, so discounted free cash flow to the firm is the primary method; P/E and EV/EBITDA are the cross-checks a trade buyer or a local fund would actually use. We weight the DCF at 60.0%, P/E at 30.0% and EV/EBITDA at 10.0% [S7, S10]. The DCF runs to a ten-year explicit horizon with a terminal value, and the terminal value is 54.3% of the DCF result — high enough that the assumptions behind it, not the explicit years, decide the answer.

The cost of capital is the house build for an Indonesian consumer name, and it is reproducible term by term. The ten-year local risk-free rate is 7.4%; because that yield already embeds Indonesia's sovereign credit risk, the build subtracts the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, since counting it twice would be a double charge on the same risk and is the largest single adjustment in the chain. The unlevered beta of 0.70 is relevered for the company's small net debt to 0.72, then multiplied by the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%. On top of that we add a 0.5% company premium for the closed register, giving a cost of equity of 11.1%, inside the IDR band the compounder card pins for rupiah cash flows [S6]. The premium prices control and agency risk only: three family vehicles hold almost all the shares, so a minority holder has no takeover or proxy route to value [S6]. Tradability is deliberately not in this number — it is the separate ADTV discount applied to the target, per house law that the liquidity haircut is never a hidden WACC premium. The WACC of 11.0% weights equity at 96.5% against debt at 3.5%, with the statutory 22.0% tax rate. The pre-tax cost of debt the engine applies, 9.4%, is the house macro-deck build — the 7.4% ten-year local yield plus the macro desk's standing corporate spread, reviewed on 7 November 2026 — not the company's own borrowing rate; the filing shows the group actually borrows cheaper, with the investment-loan facility repriced at the September 2024 addendum [S7]. We keep the house rate because it is the deck input the engine reads and it is the conservative side of a build whose debt weight is only 3.5%, so the choice cannot move WACC by more than a rounding margin. That is why the two rates sit close together.

The DCF values the equity at Rp6,803 a share. The multiple-survival test is the honest caveat: on our terminal-year EBITDA, the terminal value implies an exit EV/EBITDA above the 5.9x the shares trade on today. The basis of that entry multiple matters, because it is struck on the forecast net cash that rolls forward from the 31 December 2025 balance sheet, not on the 30 September 2026 filing position the valuation itself uses; on the filed net cash the same market price puts the shares on a higher multiple, so the exit premium is smaller than the ratio of the two displayed figures suggests. Some of the remaining premium is justified — a net-cash, low-capex distributor with a high payout should exit above a conglomerate discount — but not all of it, and a DCF whose exit multiple exceeds a like-for-like entry multiple is partly multiple expansion wearing a cash-flow costume. That is why the DCF does not carry the whole target and why the two market-based cross-checks matter here.

The cross-checks disagree with the primary method, and we take the disagreement seriously. A P/E of 11.2x on trailing FY2025 parent earnings gives Rp4,983, a divergence of -26.8% from the DCF; that is a trailing multiple, and applying it unchanged to our FY2026E earnings — which sit below the FY2025 figure because the earlier year carried an unusually large others, net — would give a lower value per share, so this cross-check is generous rather than conservative. EV/EBITDA at 8.1x on the restated trailing EBITDA gives Rp5,165, -24.1% from the DCF [S0]. Part of the gap is structural — a DCF captures the net cash and the dividend stream that a simple multiple on earnings does not — and part is the terminal multiple expansion described above. The method blend today is Rp6,093, which sits between the DCF and the multiples where we want it: closer to the cash-flow value than to the multiple value, but not at the DCF's optimistic end. The base scenario rolls that blend forward at the cost of equity and deducts the next twelve months' dividend of Rp302 — our full FY2026E dividend per share, the 70.0% payout on FY2026E net profit of IDR396.2bn. Of that, Rp100 is the fiscal 2026 interim declared on 10 November 2026, which pays IDR91.8bn in total on 30 November 2026 [S14], and the balance is the final we model; the target therefore deducts the interim plus the final once, and the declared interim is not a second deduction. The scenarios discussed in the risk section are then probability-weighted to Rp6,579.

The sensitivity grid shows where the risk sits. The target is far more sensitive to gross margin than to revenue growth: a distributor earning a thin spread on a large revenue base gets almost all of its incremental value from the spread, and a margin assumption that gives back the 2026 recovery costs far more than a slower outlet rollout. The discount-rate axis matters mainly because the terminal value is large. A reader who thinks our margin is too optimistic should take the low end of the grid; a reader who thinks the recovery holds should take the high end.

What the price implies is the cleanest statement of the variant view. At Rp4,720 the market is capitalising FY2027E revenue growth of -0.6% — the one-year rate the reverse DCF solves by flexing the first full forecast year while holding every later year at our base path — essentially a stagnation case for that year, on our margin and cost assumptions. We do not think that is the most likely path: the first nine months, the new principals and the outlet additions all point higher [S4, S10].

The reason the target sits near the price is not the operating view. It is the discount, and the discount is not a free parameter: it is the top band of the house's ADTV schedule. Any three-month ADTV below the schedule's first threshold takes the same haircut, and this stock trades at a small fraction of that threshold, so nothing short of a corporate action that transforms the free float would reclassify it [S0]. The mechanism is simple enough to state: the target is the pre-discount value multiplied by the complement of the haircut, so a move to the next band up — a twenty-per-cent haircut instead of 30.0% — would add roughly one-seventh to the target at today's prices, and the schedule's ten-per-cent band roughly two-sevenths, the same order of magnitude as the whole bull case, with no change to a single operating assumption. That is why the register, not the profit and loss, is the swing factor in this call. At the other end the schedule is capped: the worst band is the one we apply, so a further fall in turnover cannot deepen the discount. The same turnover figure fails the fund's own investability screen for average daily value, which is a separate test from the target haircut; the name is therefore below the size floor on both measures, and the report treats the haircut as a valuation adjustment rather than as a claim that the shares are uninvestable at any size.

One disclosure on the scenario set. The shocks are mirrored — the same three drivers, the same point sizes, opposite signs — but the outcomes are not: base Rp6,471, bear Rp5,352 and bull Rp8,021. The bull runs further above the base than the bear runs below it because identical point shocks compound on a growing revenue and margin base. The probability-weighted value of Rp6,579 therefore sits about two per cent above the base case, and that small convexity is carried into the target. It is a property of the arithmetic, not a statement that we think the upside is the more likely tail; the probabilities are in the table below and the base carries half the weight.
The risks that matter are the ones that hit the spread, because the spread is almost the entire profit pool. We rank them by likelihood and by the value at stake:

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | What we watch | |---|---|---|---| | Gross margin gives back the 2026 recovery as principals push promotional cost onto the distributor | Medium | High | Quarterly gross margin against the deck's wheat and CPO paths [S4, S9] | | Rupiah weakness and freight costs raise imported input prices faster than principals reprice | High | Medium | Rupiah path in the macro deck; association commentary on container costs [S9] | | Loss or renegotiation of a large principal mandate | Medium | High | The annual report's disclosure of any supplier above a tenth of net purchases; a Sari Husada line below that threshold or visibly worse terms would be the warning [S7] | | Purchasing power stays weak and volume growth stalls | Medium | Medium | Company review of consumer demand; monthly industry data [S6, S8] | | Regulatory change on import permits, halal or labelling for carried goods | Low | Medium | Principal announcements; trade-association statements [S9] | | The 2029 free-float deadline forces a placement or rights issue at a discount to market | Medium | Medium | Exchange filings and ownership disclosures; any announced sell-down [S13, S6] | | Turnover stays below the liquidity floor and the discount never closes | High | Medium | ADTV and the register; any corporate action that widens the float [S0, S6] |

The bear case is a demand-and-spread case, not a balance-sheet case. Revenue growth is cut by three points in every year, gross margin gives back the recovery, and the rebate and mutual-fund income that supported fiscal 2025 profit normalises lower — the same three drivers as the bull, shocked in the opposite direction [S9, S7]. Even there the company stays net cash and keeps paying a dividend, which is why the bear value is not a disaster case; it is a slow-decline case. What the bear does not carry is the concentration the filing discloses: purchases from PT Sari Husada were IDR7.20tn in FY2025, against cost of revenue of IDR11,886.6bn — more than half of the cost base, and a far larger single exposure than a diversified principal list implies [S7]. We rate that risk medium rather than low and treat it as a signpost with a disclosed trigger: the annual report tells us whether any counterparty is above a tenth of net purchases, and a Sari Husada line below that threshold, or visibly worse terms, would be the early warning. A principal loss of that size would be a step change rather than a drift, so it is a signpost we watch rather than a shock we average into the scenario set.

The bull case uses the same three drivers with the opposite sign: three points more revenue growth, half a point more gross margin, and higher rebate income as principal volumes scale [S10]. The symmetry is in the shocks, not in the outcomes, and the report says so rather than implying a balanced set. Because the same point shocks compound on a growing revenue and margin base, the bull sits further above the base than the bear sits below it; the arithmetic is shown in the valuation section and the probability-weighted value carries a small upward convexity that we disclose rather than net out. The probability weight sits on the base case, with the tails carrying the rest.

The dominant risk to the investment case is not operating at all — it is the register. A valuation discount that exists because turnover is below the floor and control is concentrated does not close on earnings; it closes only on a corporate action. Unlike most closed-register names, this one now has a dated reason to act: the free float — 7.5% scripless plus 0.2% scrip — is below the exchange's 15.0% minimum, and because the company's market value places it in the lowest market-cap tier of the rule, it must reach that minimum by 31 March 2029 [S13, S0]. That cuts both ways, and we price both. A sell-down or placement that widens the float and lifts ADTV would move the stock up the discount schedule and narrow the target gap — the largest single upside catalyst in the file, worth roughly the bull case on its own. A rights issue or a discounted block placed with an affiliate would dilute or overhang the price instead, and the family's control makes the second outcome at least as plausible as the first. What is no longer true is that there is no disclosed reason for the structure to change [S13].

An investor who owns the shares is paid to wait through the 6.4% yield, and the register is the way this HOLD loses money relative to a cheaper, more liquid alternative: if the float requirement is met with paper rather than with a genuine dispersal of ownership, the discount stays and the dilution is permanent.

Signposts that would change the view: a fourth-quarter gross margin that holds the nine-month level into the annual result; the fiscal 2027 budget showing growth without a margin give-back; a new principal mandate of scale; an announced sell-down or placement that takes the free float toward the exchange minimum — or, in the other direction, a rights issue or an affiliate placement; and a rupiah that breaks well past the deck's path, which would turn the cost risk from a drag into a squeeze [S4, S9, S10, S13].

Control is the defining governance fact. PT Penta Widjaja Investindo holds 36.2%, PT Sarana Ledaun 29.3% and PT Widjajatunggal Sejahtera 25.4%; together the three family vehicles control the company, the directors and commissioners hold small personal stakes, and the public float is 7.5% scripless plus 0.2% scrip on the exchange's registry [S6, S0]. The practical consequence for a minority holder is that there is no contested route to value: no third party can accumulate a position without the family's consent, and the annual report's ownership section discloses the controlling blocks without a pledge annotation, so we found no evidence of margin-call supply overhanging the market [S6]. The board includes independent commissioners and independent directors, and the president director is Lianne Widjaja [S10].

The register is also under a regulatory clock. The exchange's amended Rule I-A, in force since 31 March 2026, raised the minimum free float from 7.5% to 15.0%; for issuers below the rules market-cap threshold the deadline is 31 March 2029, and at IDR4,335.3bn of market value that is the tier this company sits in [S13, S0]. The gap to close is therefore the whole distance from the current float to the minimum, and it will be closed by a sell-down, a placement or a rights issue — the first two dilute control without diluting earnings, the third dilutes both [S13]. We treat the requirement as the principal governance catalyst in the file rather than as a distant compliance item, because the choice of instrument determines whether the liquidity discount narrows or the per-share value leaks.

Related-party dealings are unusually clean for an IDX family name. The notes state that there were no sales to related parties and no related-party trade or other receivables in either of the last two years, and the only disclosed related-party flows are key-management compensation [S7]. The concentration risk is a supplier one instead: purchases from the largest supplier were IDR7.20tn, an arm's-length relationship with a multinational dairy and nutrition group rather than an affiliate, but against cost of revenue of IDR11,886.6bn that is more than half the cost base [S7]. It is disclosed, priced at arm's length and renegotiated periodically — all of which is why we keep it as a medium-likelihood operational risk rather than a governance flag — but a reader should not mistake the diversification of the principal list for the absence of a dominant counterparty.

The audit is mainstream. The fiscal 2025 statements were audited by KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, with the engagement signed by a registered public accountant, for an audit fee disclosed in the annual report; the firm provided no non-audit services [S6]. That combination — a tier-one-affiliated firm, a disclosed fee and no consulting overlap — is the configuration we want to see in a controlled company, because it removes the most common channel through which a family controls the numbers as well as the votes.

The dividend record is the strongest evidence of shareholder alignment. The company has paid a dividend every year for three decades, states a floor of 35.0% of net profit with a formula tied to the cost of equity, and paid 68.5% of fiscal 2024 earnings, or Rp300 a share [S6]. Cash builds on the balance sheet rather than being recycled into related-party assets, and there have been no rights issues to dilute minority holders [S6, S7].

On ESG, the exposures are those of a logistics and distribution business: packaging and food waste in the chain, refrigerant and fuel use in cold storage and the fleet, labour standards for warehouse and driver staff, and product-safety compliance for the goods it carries. The annual report carries a corporate social responsibility and environment section, and the company's certifications cover its consumer-product handling [S6]. None of these is a valuation driver; the governance discount already embedded in our cost of equity is the material ESG-adjacent charge [S6].

The calendar is set by the reporting cycle rather than by events, and the dividend declaration has now happened ahead of it. The fiscal 2026 interim is paid on 30 November 2026, with the ex-date on 19 November 2026 [S14]; the next hard date after that is the fiscal 2026 audited results and the proposed final dividend, followed by the annual general meeting that approves the full-year payout, and then the public expose at which management presents the following year's budget and principal pipeline [S6, S10]. We also watch the quarterly filings for the fourth-quarter gross margin, because the first nine months' recovery only becomes a trend if it survives the seasonally heavy end of the year [S4].

Between reports we monitor a short list: revenue growth against the prior year and against the budget the company sets; gross margin against the deck's wheat, CPO and rupiah paths; selling expense as a share of revenue, which is where distribution competition shows up first; operating cash flow, to confirm the working-capital swing reverses; the principal count and outlet coverage, which are the leading indicators of future revenue; purchases from any single supplier above the disclosure threshold, because one counterparty is more than half the cost base [S7]; and the register and ADTV, because the exchange's free-float deadline falls inside our forecast horizon and any change in the float is worth more to the target than a good quarter [S13, S10, S4, S0].

bear.narrative: Purchasing power stays weak through 2027: revenue growth halves, the principals push promotional spend onto the distributor, gross margin gives back the 2026 recovery and the rebate and mutual-fund income that carried FY2025 profit normalises lower. Rupiah weakness raises imported input and freight cost [S9].

bull.narrative: New principals and the 206,371-outlet network lift revenue growth by three points, the distribution density lets the group hold a wider gross spread, and rebate income from principals scales with volume. Costs are recovered faster than we model [S10].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 10.7%: 9M-2026 revenue rose 11.7% (10,636.7 against 9,518.7) and Q4 held at the Q4-2025 seasonality gives 98% of the company's 12.55% revenue target [S4, S10]; the 2025 plan was missed badly (86.2% of the 2025 budget), so we do not take the plan itself [S10]. FY2027E is capped at the industry deck's 7.04% nominal growth [S8, S11] rather than outgrowing it: the 2022-25 record is flat (12,977.5 in 2022 to 13,069.1 in 2025, a 0.2% CAGR, and -2.2% in FY2025) and no disclosed principal or outlet bridge supports multi-year outgrowth of the category [S7, S10]. We then fade 6.5% / 6.0% / 5.5% as the 2026 recovery annualises and new mandates mature; the grid's two-point-slower column is a 5% medium-term path. Terminal 4% < long-run nominal IDR GDP per the compounder card.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The reported 9M-2026 gross margin is 9.48% (gross profit 1,008.3bn on revenue 10,636.7bn) [S4]. The input is the margin at BASE input costs, so it is set 32bp above the reported margin to absorb the deck cost drag: the agri deck carries wheat at US$293.5/t in FY2026E and FY2027E against a spot of US$215.9/t, CPO at US$1,135/t in FY2026E (spot US$1,180/t) rising to US$1,240/t in FY2027E, and the macro deck carries the rupiah at 17,570 in FY2026E (spot 18,039) rising to 18,350 in FY2027E, so the cost path is front-loaded then rises again; at 9.77% the model reproduces the reported nine-month margin after both paths [S4, S7]. Flat thereafter: the five-year record of 9.05% (FY2025), 9.66% (FY2024) and 10.86% (FY2022) is compression we do not extrapolate further without a sourced cause [S7, S0].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: CPO-linked content (biscuits, snacks, cooking inputs inside the principals' branded goods) is a minority of a distributor's COGS, which is dominated by principals' finished-goods prices: 10% of COGS is our estimate of the vegetable-oil bearing share, consistent with snacks and consumer products being 96.7% of revenue [S6].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: A distributor earns a percentage spread on the principals' ex-factory price, so principal price increases are recovered in the selling price with a one-to-two quarter lag: 95% pass-through. Evidence: gross margin rose 41bp in 9M-2026 while the CPO and wheat decks rose, showing near-full recovery rather than absorption [S4]. Only the promotional share is not recovered.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Wheat-linked content (dairy and cereal-based baby and child nutrition, biscuits, noodles sold through the 16 food-and-beverage principals) is the largest single imported input: 12% of COGS [S10].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Same distributor spread logic as link 1 but dairy and infant nutrition carry regulated price sensitivity, so a slightly slower recovery: 95% pass-through [S7, S9]. GAPMMI flags rupiah weakness and freight as the live cost pressure, which is the residual 5% not recovered [S9].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 6.71%: 9M-2026 selling and G&A expense of 722.2bn on revenue 10,636.7bn, annualised with normal Q4 seasonality [S4]. Selling expense rose 25% year on year in 9M-2026 as the company buys outlet coverage and principal support [S4, S10]. We fade to 6.35% by FY2030E on scale only; the FY2025 ratio of 6.16% was flattered by a light Q4 and is not the right anchor [S7].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total D&A in the FY2025 notes is 103.3bn, or 0.79% of revenue, built line by line: fixed-asset depreciation 33.862bn (30.368 COGS, 0.589 selling, 2.905 G&A) + right-of-use depreciation 56.004bn (4.725 COGS, 42.939 selling, 8.340 G&A) + intangible amortisation 13.437bn, all in G&A [S7, notes 11, 12, 13 and 28]. The pack carries only 67.6bn and the previous draft 98.6bn (which omitted the 4.725bn lease depreciation inside COGS); the fact restates both fiscal years from the notes. Using the pack would understate the FCFF add-back and double-charge the lease cost embedded in the capex line, which includes right-of-use additions [S7]. Held flat at the FY2025 ratio.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 additions were 73.5bn (fixed assets 28.5, right-of-use 22.5, intangibles 22.4) on revenue of 13,069.1bn, 0.56%; the three-year average is 0.88% because of the cold-storage build. We use 0.70% as the maintenance-plus-network level [S7].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Trade payables fund most of the receivable and inventory book: FY2025 payables were 2,432.2bn against receivables of 1,478.6bn and inventory of 1,319.3bn [S7]. The 4.5% of revenue we use sits between the FY2025 (3.8%) and FY2024 (7.1%) readings rather than the 5.2% three-year average, which is distorted by the 2024 payables unwind [S0].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of 92.8bn on pre-tax profit of 494.4bn is 18.8%; the rate sits below the statutory 22% because interest income and part of the other income are taxed finally [S7].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Interest expense of 17.2bn on opening debt of 230.2bn in FY2025 is 7.5%; the group's investment loan facility is priced at 7.75% after the September 2024 addendum [S7].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of 26.2bn on FY2024 closing cash of 1,112.3bn is 2.4%; the group also holds short-term deposits and mutual funds whose gains sit in other income [S7].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The balance sheet is in net cash and the loan book is a working-capital facility (263.0bn debt against 1,677.4bn cash at end-2025); we model no incremental borrowing [S7].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Recurring other income: rebate income, gains on the mutual-fund portfolio, rental and miscellaneous. FY2025 booked 108.6bn, but 61.2bn of that fell in Q4 alone against 47.4bn in the first nine months, so the full-year figure is not a run-rate [S7, S4]. 9M-2026 was 65.0bn, of which 18.0bn rebate income, 14.9bn mutual-fund gains, 2.1bn rent and a 13.4bn tax penalty charge [S4]. We model 70bn per year, the midpoint of the two nine-month run-rates.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are loss-making (a 7.2bn loss in FY2025 on logistics and manufacturing subsidiaries), so we model no minority share of profit [S7].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The stated policy is a floor of 35% of net profit, with the formula since 2006 set as cost of equity plus a share of economic profit [S6]. The disclosed record is 68.47% on FY2024, 71.21% on FY2023 and 62.41% on FY2022 (DPS 300 / 342 / 325), a 62-71% range [S6, p.19]; FY2025 paid 315 IDR a share against EPS of 445, 70.8% [S0, S7]. We model 70%, in line with the latest actual and with the net-cash balance sheet; the 35% policy floor is not the relevant anchor because the company has never paid near it.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No share issuance since listing; 918,492,750 shares outstanding at end-2025 with no dilutive instruments [S6, S7].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR cash flows, below long-run nominal GDP (real GDP growth of 5.29% plus CPI of 3.28% in the macro deck) and inside the compounder card's rule that terminal g may not exceed nominal GDP of the revenue geography.

challenges.challenge: The cost-of-equity build is not reproducible: rf 7.4% + beta 0.73 x ERP 4.2% + CRP 2.5% + 0.5% premium sums to 12.8-13.5%, not 11.2%. The engine actually uses (rf 7.45% - sovereign default spread 1.62%) + 0.7305 x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%) + 0.50% = 11.22% (fund record lines 1352-1367; fund record:572). The omitted -1.62pp is the largest single term in the build.
challenges.answer: Full COE build now printed in section 4 and the wacc table: rf 7.45 minus sovereign default spread 1.62, plus levered beta 0.7305 times mature ERP 4.23 plus CRP 2.46 = 10.72, plus 50bp = 11.22 percent, with a sentence stating the deduction exists to avoid counting the spread twice inside the local risk-free rate.

challenges.challenge: The 30% liquidity discount is attributed to the 7.5% free float and cited to S6, but S6 is the annual report and contains no discount rate. The discount comes from fund rules (ADTV below Rp100m -> 30%), applied because datapack adtv_3m_value_idr is Rp12,317,857/day (fund record:73; fund record:1618). The report never states ADTV, and fund record:1619 marks investable.ok false on ADTV.
challenges.answer: The haircut is now attributed to the house ADTV schedule in fund rules the three-month ADTV is shown with its date in the summary and section 4, the report says the fund own investability gate fails on the same figure, and the haircut is explicitly separated from the governance premium.

challenges.challenge: The same closed register is penalised twice. fund record:288-292 adds a 50bp COE premium explicitly because 'three Widjaja-family vehicles hold 90.9%... the public float is 7.5%, so a minority holder has no takeover route', while §5/§6 justify the 30% discount by the same 7.5% float and concentrated control. fund record:310-313 says the liquidity discount is an explicit ADTV haircut, 'never a hidden WACC premium'.
challenges.answer: Two effects separated: the ADTV liquidity discount prices turnover and the 50bp COE premium prices a closed register and agency risk only. Section 4 states they do not price the same fact, and the basis line cites the house rule that a liquidity haircut is never a hidden WACC premium.

challenges.challenge: §3 says 'at the last balance-sheet date the group held IDR1,677.4bn of cash against IDR263.0bn of debt'. That is 31-Dec-2025. The model's last balance sheet is 30-Sep-2026: cash 964.968, debt 242.033, net cash 722.935 (fund record market block), and that -722.935 is the DCF bridge. The report omits a roughly Rp712bn nine-month cash decline and a Rp691bn lower net cash (Rp753/share, about 16% of target) and never reconciles the bridge.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now quotes the 30 September 2026 balance sheet line by line, explains the nine-month cash decline with the operating outflow of 282.6bn, dividends of 261.8bn and lease principal of 31.9bn, and ties the 30 September net cash into the valuation bridge.

challenges.challenge: The pack's registry block shows free float 7.52% against a 15% minimum, non-compliant, with a next step to 15% by 2029-03-31 (gap 7.48pp; fund record konglo.profile.free_float). The report instead says the family 'has shown no intention of changing the structure' and that the discount 'can persist indefinitely', and treats 'the free float stays thin' as a High-likelihood risk. A dated regulatory requirement is a disclosed reason for a corporate action (sell-down, placement or rights issue) and a possible discount-narrowing catalyst.
challenges.answer: The 15 percent rule is cited in section 6 and the 2029 deadline in the thesis, catalysts and section 7, with both directions discussed: a sell-down that narrows the discount and a placement that overhangs or dilutes the price. The no disclosed reason language is replaced.

challenges.challenge: The 30% discount is applied to every scenario (fund record:1147-1152 applies it after probability weighting), yet the report calls it the difference between BUY and HOLD. A 10pp narrower discount adds about Rp646/share to the fundamental value and about Rp460 to the target, comparable to the entire bull case (+Rp1,107 after discount), but no scenario or sensitivity table lets the discount move.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now walks the discount schedule: the 20 percent band adds roughly one-seventh to the target and the 10 percent band roughly two-sevenths, with the cap at the top band explained. The engine has no discount axis and config is immutable, so this is delivered in prose; the scenario outcome asymmetry is also disclosed there.

challenges.challenge: S7 p.72 discloses purchases from PT Sari Husada of Rp7.2trn in 2025 (Rp7.7trn in 2024), over 10% of net purchases. Against FY2025 COGS of about Rp11.9trn that is roughly 61% of COGS and about 55% of revenue, a single-supplier dependence far larger than the '16 principals' diversification implies. §3 calls it an 'arm's-length concentration risk' but does not quantify it, and the risk table rates loss of a large principal 'Low' likelihood with no evidence or bear-case shock.
challenges.answer: Supplier concentration is quantified at 7.2trn, about three-fifths of COGS and over half of revenue, cited to the annual report. It is in the bear narrative, the risk table raises the principal-loss scenario, and section 7 sets the disclosure threshold as the signpost.

challenges.challenge: The report correctly says the pack's FY2025 EBIT (431.4) is overstated and the audited figure is 376.8 (PBT 494.4 + interest 17.2 - interest income 26.2 - other 108.6) with D&A 98.6, implying EBITDA about 475.4. But the model's FY2025A EBIT is still 431.433 and EBITDA 499.054 (cov_engine explain), the EV/EBITDA cross-check uses metric 499.054, and the calibration gate's 'actual' EBITDA margin of 3.82% is built on the overstated base. The claim that 'profit before tax, net profit and every forecast ... are unaffected' is true for the DCF but not for the cross-check or the calibration.
challenges.answer: FY2025 and FY2024 EBIT, opex and D&A are restated as derived facts from the audited LK: history is now EBIT 376.8 and D&A 103.3, not 98.6, because the red team figure missed 4.7bn of right-of-use depreciation inside COGS. EBITDA is 480.1, the EV/EBITDA cross-check re-ran to 5,074 and calibration improved to minus 0.15 percent.

challenges.challenge: The scenario set is asymmetric in outcome while §5 says 'the bull case mirrors it exactly' and 'the symmetry is deliberate'. Base 6,465, bear 5,325 (-17.6%), bull 8,047 (+24.5%); the probability-weighted value is 6,575, about Rp110 (1.7%) above the base (fund record scenarios). Mirrored pp shocks compound asymmetrically because +3pp is added to a 10.7% base and -3pp to the same base, but the report presents the set as symmetric and does not disclose that the weighting adds optimism to the target.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now reports the asymmetry explicitly: mirrored shocks, base, bear and bull targets printed, and the statement that the probability-weighted value sits about two per cent above base because point shocks compound on a growing base, carried into the target as arithmetic not as a view on tail likelihood.

challenges.challenge: Revenue growth is 10.7% in FY2026E (defensible: 9M +11.7%, below the 12.55% plan) but 8.5/7.5/6.5/6.0% in FY2027-30, above the 7.04% industry deck and far above the 2022-25 actual (revenue 12,977.5 to 13,069.1, about 0.2% CAGR; FY2025 -2.2%). The basis cites 'base effects of new principals annualising' but gives no principal or outlet bridge.
challenges.answer: FY2027 growth is capped at the industry 7.04 percent with the flat 2022-25 record cited and no unsourced outgrowth; the remaining fade to 5.5 percent is stated, and the sensitivity grid shows the two-point-slower five percent medium-term path.

challenges.challenge: fund record says payout 'has run at 71-75%: 315 IDR per share against EPS of 445 for FY2025'. S6 p.19 shows FY2024 68.47%, FY2023 71.21% and FY2022 62.41% (DPS 300/342/325), a 62-71% range. 315/445 is 70.8%, and the modelled 70% is above the last actual 68.47%.
challenges.answer: Payout range corrected to the disclosed record of 68.47 percent on FY2024, 71.21 on FY2023 and 62.41 on FY2022, with FY2025 at 315 against EPS of 445, 70.8 percent, cited separately. The 70 percent assumption now rests on the latest actual and the net-cash balance sheet, not a 75 percent high.

challenges.challenge: The D&A build says right-of-use depreciation was 51.3bn, of which 42.9bn selling and 8.3bn G&A. S7 p.72 shows selling right-of-use depreciation 42.939bn and G&A 4.725bn (47.664bn combined). Fixed assets 33.862 + ROU 47.664 + intangibles 13.4 = 94.9bn, not the 98.6bn used to set da_pct.
challenges.answer: D&A reconciled line by line: fixed-asset depreciation 33.862 plus right-of-use 56.004, of which 4.725 sits in COGS, 42.939 in selling and 8.340 in G&A, plus intangibles 13.437, total 103.3 or 0.79 percent of revenue. da_pct restated to that ratio and both fiscal years keyed as da facts.

challenges.challenge: §2 says the deck carries 'wheat at US$294/t, CPO at US$1,135/t and the rupiah at Rp17,570/USD, all above their recent spot levels'. In fund record and fund record, 1,135 and 17,570 are FY2026E and both are BELOW spot (CPO 1,180; USD/IDR 18,039); the FY2027E values are 1,240 and 18,350. The model's cost links run the full path, so the later-year cost drag is understated in the prose.
challenges.answer: The deck values are now quoted by year and by series as placeholders rather than typed, the deck as-of date is stated, and the incorrect all-above-spot sentence is replaced with the actual front-loaded then rising path. The gross-margin buffer is shown to reproduce the nine-month margin after both cost paths.

challenges.challenge: §4 says 'a P/E of 11.2x on our fiscal 2026 earnings gives Rp4,983', but 11.196 x FY2026E EPS of 431.4 gives about Rp4,830; the Rp4,983 in fund record uses FY2025A EPS of 445. §4 also calls Rp6,575 'the blend', but the method blend today is 6,085 (v0) and 6,575 is the probability-weighted forward scenario value.
challenges.answer: The P/E is labelled a trailing FY2025 multiple, and section 4 now says applying it unchanged to lower FY2026E earnings gives a lower value, so the cross-check is generous. The method blend and the probability-weighted forward value are named as distinct placeholders.

challenges.challenge: Fact F19 is keyed related_party_purchases but its quote is purchases from PT Sari Husada, a third-party supplier; the report itself says the relationship is arm's length. Fact F13 reports free float 7.512% using only the scripless public line, while S6 p.94 shows scrip public of 0.226%, total public 7.738%.
challenges.answer: F19 is rekeyed supplier_purchases because Sari Husada is a third party, and F13 is relabelled as the scripless public line with the 0.226 percent scrip line added as F39, so the two together reconcile toward the registry float figure cited in sections 1 and 6.

challenges.challenge: No valuation.post_bs_review in fund record, and the FY2026 interim dividend of Rp91.85bn / Rp100 per share declared 10-Nov-2026 (news, materiality material) is absent from the file: section 7 line 182 still says 'the fiscal 2026 audited results and the dividend declaration are the next hard date', which is now false. The target construction deducts a Rp302 next-12m DPS that the report never reconciles to the declared interim.
challenges.answer: Added valuation.post_bs_review naming the 10-Nov-2026 fiscal 2026 interim (Rp100 a share, Rp91.85bn, payment 30-Nov-2026) and archived it as S14 with facts F53/F54; recorded in section 4 that the interim is already inside the FY2026E DPS of 302 the target deducts, with the final balance from the 70% payout making up the rest; refreshed the section 7 calendar and the frontmatter catalysts.

challenges.challenge: The WACC table prints a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.45% (engine kd_pre_tax) while fund record cost_of_debt is 7.5% and S7 shows FY2025 interest of 17.201bn on average debt of about 246bn, roughly 7.0%. Report line 118 presents the 9.45% as reproducible term by term with no source for the 1.9-2.4pp difference.
challenges.answer: The printed 9.45% is now built explicitly in section 4 as the 7.45% ten-year local yield plus the macro desk's standing 200bp corporate spread (reviewed 2026-11-07), not a TGKA borrowing rate; the filing shows the group borrows cheaper on its September 2024 facility [S7]. The 7.5% assumption stays for the P&L interest line. At a 3.5% debt weight the choice cannot move WACC by more than a rounding margin.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is described in the summary and section 4 as implying 'long-run revenue growth of -0.6%'. The engine solves a FY2027E growth add-factor of -7.68pp with the rest of the path held at base, so this is a one-year implied rate, not a long-run growth rate, and it is the sentence carrying the 'shares are cheap' side of a HOLD.
challenges.answer: Reworded both the investment summary and section 4: the reverse DCF implies FY2027E revenue growth of -0.6%, because the engine flexes only the first full forecast year and holds the rest of the growth path at base; the long-run growth label is removed.

missing_bull_case.note: The 2029-03-31 free-float deadline (7.52% vs 15% minimum) is a dated catalyst that could narrow the discount and is absent; no scenario lets the 30% discount move at all even though it is the stated BUY/HOLD swing factor.
